question.text: 5/10: _mEghadUtam_ is a _khanDakAvya_ (“short poem”) and begins with the word _kaschit_ (“any”). _kumArasambhavam_ is a _mahAkAvya_ (“epic poem”) and begins with the word _asti_ (“is”). The story goes that Kalidasa chose those opening words carefully. Per this lore, he is a particularly stupid villager who gets married off to an intelligent princess because of the scheming of a spurned courtier. The princess asks her new husband, “_asti kaschit vAgviSEshah_?” (“is there any special erudition within you?”), which he promptly fails to understand. After some intense melodrama and divine intervention by Kali, he becomes a great poet, and he decides to compose works beginning with each of those taunting words. question.text: He was born in Hyderabad state on October 22, 1901 to a Gondi family. In his boyhood years, the Nizamate increased mining activities in Adivasi areas, and his father was killed by forest officials for opposing mining. He joined his people’s fight for their rights, and around the age of 20, he escaped arrest and fled to Assam where he worked on a tea plantation. He got involved with a labor union there and was arrested; he escaped jail and went back to Hyderabad state. After failed attempts to redress political grievances through petitions, he joined the banned Communist Party of India and started an armed rebellion. He was killed in 1940 in a police encounter. His slogan was “Jal, Jangal, Zameen.” He is now worshipped as a deity by the Gond people and his death anniversary is observed on the full moon day in the month of Asvayuja (Ashvin). A district of Telangana was named after him a few years ago. Who?

question.text: The mathematical notion of limit and the closely related notion of convergence are central to any modern definition of integration. In the 19th century, Karl Weierstrass developed the rigorous epsilon-delta definition of a limit, which is still accepted and used by mathematicians today. He built on previous but non-rigorous work by Augustin Cauchy, who had used the non-standard notion of infinitesimally small numbers, today rejected in standard mathematical analysis. Before Cauchy, Bernard Bolzano had laid the fundamental groundwork of the epsilon-delta definition. X followed up on this by formalizing what is now called the X integral. To define this integral, one fills the area under the graph with smaller and smaller rectangles and takes the limit of the sums of the areas of the rectangles at each stage. For some functions, however, the total area of these rectangles does not approach a single number. Thus, they have no X integral. Who is X, you will also know him for a famous unsolved problem?
